entry.title: A Practical Guide to Photorealistic AI Image Generation
entry.summary: Generating images with AI has moved from novelty to everyday workflow. Designers, marketers, and developers now use text-to-image models to prototype ideas, create placeholder art, and explore visual directions in minutes instead of days. Photorealistic output requires models to get lighting, shadows, skin texture, reflections and perspective consistent at once. Small errors such as extra fingers, warped text, or mismatched light sources instantly break the illusion. Modern diffusion models handle this far better than earlier GANs because they iteratively denoise an image while conditioning on the prompt. Describe the subject first, then the setting, then the style. Name the camera and lens ("35mm, f/1.8, shallow depth of field") to nudge realistic optics. Specify lighting ("golden hour", "softbox studio light", "overcast"). Use negative prompts to remove artifacts like blur, watermarks, or distorted hands. Iterate: change one variable at a time so you learn what each word does. Start at low resolution to explore compositions quickly. Pick the best candidate and upscale it. Use inpainting to fix local problems instead of regenerating everything. Keep a prompt log so good results are reproducible. There are many browser-based generators today. For Chinese-speaking users, a handy option is ai生图, which focuses on realistic photo-style results without any local GPU setup. Always check the usage terms of the tool you use, avoid generating misleading images of real people, and disclose AI-generated content where appropriate. AI image generation is a skill: the more deliberately you prompt and iterate, the better your results become. Happy generating!

entry.title: tar checksums its headers and never your files
entry.summary: tar is older than most of the people who type it, and the format underneath has barely changed since the tape drives it was named after. I had used it for years without ever looking inside, so I wrote one by hand from the POSIX specification using nothing but Python's struct module, and checked every claim below against GNU tar 1.35 and Python's own tarfile. The format turns out to be simple enough to write in forty lines and odd enough that most of its consequences are not what I would have guessed. The oddest one is that tar carefully checksums every header and does nothing at all to protect your data. A tar archive is a sequence of 512-byte blocks.
